claim: Inputs from the ventral hippocampus (vHIP) to the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) are implicated in several neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Inputs from the ventral hippocampus (vHIP) to the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) are implicated in several neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that references established knowledge in the field about the vHIP-mPFC projection and neuropsychiatric disorders.

claim: The vHIP-mPFC projection is hyperactive in the Mecp2 knockout mouse model of Rett syndrome.
source: Here, we show that the vHIP-mPFC projection is hyperactive in the Mecp2 knockout mouse model of the autism spectrum disorder Rett syndrome, which has deficits in social memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including voltage-sensitive dye imaging and electrophysiological recordings showing enhanced vHIP-mPFC signaling in Mecp2 KO mice.

claim: Mecp2 knockout mice have deficits in social memory.
source: Here, we show that the vHIP-mPFC projection is hyperactive in the Mecp2 knockout mouse model of the autism spectrum disorder Rett syndrome, which has deficits in social memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the three-chamber social test and unrestricted social interaction assay showing impaired social memory in Mecp2 KO mice.

claim: Long-term excitation of mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons in wild-type mice impaired social memory.
source: Long-term excitation of mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons in wild-type mice impaired social memory, whereas their long-term inhibition in Rett mice rescued social memory deficits.
evidence: This claim is supported by chemogenetic manipulation experiments using hM3Dq DREADDs to excite vHIP-mPFC neurons, followed by behavioral testing showing impaired social memory.

claim: Long-term inhibition of mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons in Rett mice rescued social memory deficits.
source: Long-term excitation of mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons in wild-type mice impaired social memory, whereas their long-term inhibition in Rett mice rescued social memory deficits.
evidence: This claim is supported by chemogenetic manipulation experiments using hM4Di DREADDs to inhibit vHIP-mPFC neurons in Mecp2 KO mice, followed by behavioral testing showing improved social memory.

claim: The extent of social memory improvement was negatively correlated with vHIP-evoked responses in mPFC slices, on a mouse-per-mouse basis.
source: The extent of social memory improvement was negatively correlated with vHIP-evoked responses in mPFC slices, on a mouse-per-mouse basis.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between social memory discrimination indices and VSD signal amplitudes in mPFC slices from individual mice.

claim: Acute manipulations of the vHIP-mPFC projection affected social memory in a region and behavior selective manner.
source: Acute manipulations of the vHIP-mPFC projection affected social memory in a region and behavior selective manner, suggesting that proper vHIP-mPFC signaling is necessary to recall social memories.
evidence: This claim is supported by acute chemogenetic manipulation experiments showing that vHIP-mPFC, but not vHIP-NAc, projections are necessary for social memory, and that novel object recognition is not affected.

claim: Proper vHIP-mPFC signaling is necessary to recall social memories.
source: Acute manipulations of the vHIP-mPFC projection affected social memory in a region and behavior selective manner, suggesting that proper vHIP-mPFC signaling is necessary to recall social memories.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the acute manipulation experiments showing that disrupting vHIP-mPFC signaling immediately before testing affects social memory performance.

claim: There is an altered pattern of vHIP innervation of mPFC neurons in Rett mice.
source: In addition, we identified an altered pattern of vHIP innervation of mPFC neurons, and increased synaptic strength of vHIP inputs onto layer five pyramidal neurons as contributing factors of aberrant vHIP-mPFC signaling in Rett mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by trans-synaptic tracing experiments using WGA showing changes in the proportion of different neuronal subtypes innervated by vHIP axons in Mecp2 KO mice.

claim: There is increased synaptic strength of vHIP inputs onto layer five pyramidal neurons in Rett mice.
source: In addition, we identified an altered pattern of vHIP innervation of mPFC neurons, and increased synaptic strength of vHIP inputs onto layer five pyramidal neurons as contributing factors of aberrant vHIP-mPFC signaling in Rett mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation experiments showing larger EPSCs and higher AMPAR/NMDAR ratios at vHIP-mPFC synapses onto layer 5 pyramidal neurons in Mecp2 KO mice.

claim: Functional neuroimaging in human subjects has revealed that higher covariance between hippocampal activity and changes in social environment reflect better social skills.
source: Functional neuroimaging in human subjects has revealed that higher covariance between hippocampal activity and changes in social environment reflect better social skills (Tavares et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tavares et al., 2015.

claim: Perturbing neuronal activity in both dorsal CA2 and ventral CA1 hippocampal subregions impairs social memory in mouse models.
source: In mouse models, perturbing neuronal activity in both dorsal CA2 and ventral CA1 hippocampal subregions impairs social memory (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Meira et al., 2018; Okuyama et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Meira et al., 2018; Okuyama et al., 2016.

claim: Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) are characterized by difficulties in interpreting social situations and a lack of social appropriation.
source: Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) are characterized by difficulties in interpreting social situations and a lack of social appropriation (Barendse et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barendse et al., 2018 and represents established knowledge about ASDs.

claim: A common feature in mouse models of monogenic ASDs is an imbalance in synaptic excitation and inhibition (E/I) within different brain regions.
source: A common feature in mouse models of monogenic ASDs is an imbalance in synaptic excitation and inhibition (E/I) within different brain regions (Nelson and Valakh, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nelson and Valakh, 2015.

claim: Altering the E/I balance in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of mice mimics autism-like social deficits.
source: Altering the E/I balance in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of mice mimics autism-like social deficits (Yizhar et al., 2011), and restoring the E/I balance in the CNTNAP2 knockout (KO) and valproate mouse models of ASDs improves their social deficits (Brumback et al., 2018; Selimbeyoglu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yizhar et al., 2011.

claim: Restoring the E/I balance in the CNTNAP2 knockout (KO) and valproate mouse models of ASDs improves their social deficits.
source: Altering the E/I balance in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of mice mimics autism-like social deficits (Yizhar et al., 2011), and restoring the E/I balance in the CNTNAP2 knockout (KO) and valproate mouse models of ASDs improves their social deficits (Brumback et al., 2018; Selimbeyoglu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brumback et al., 2018; Selimbeyoglu et al., 2017.

claim: Excitatory pyramidal neurons of the ventral hippocampus (vHIP) send long-range projections to the mPFC.
source: Excitatory pyramidal neurons of the ventral hippocampus (vHIP) send long-range projections to the mPFC (Dégenètais et al., 2003; Dembrow et al., 2010; Liu and Carter, 2018; Thierry et al., 2000), and the activity of different populations of mPFC pyramidal neurons are correlated with the novelty of a social target (Liang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dégenètais et al., 2003; Dembrow et al., 2010; Liu and Carter, 2018; Thierry et al., 2000.

claim: The activity of different populations of mPFC pyramidal neurons are correlated with the novelty of a social target.
source: Excitatory pyramidal neurons of the ventral hippocampus (vHIP) send long-range projections to the mPFC (Dégenètais et al., 2003; Dembrow et al., 2010; Liu and Carter, 2018; Thierry et al., 2000), and the activity of different populations of mPFC pyramidal neurons are correlated with the novelty of a social target (Liang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liang et al., 2018.

claim: The Mecp2 KO mouse model exhibits heightened activity in the vHIP.
source: We focused on the Mecp2 KO mouse model of RTT because of the heightened activity in the vHIP (Calfa et al., 2011; Calfa et al., 2015) and the hypoactivity of cortical regions (Durand et al., 2012; Kron et al., 2012; Morello et al., 2018; Sceniak et al., 2016; Tomassy et al., 2014), both resulting from opposite changes in their microcircuit E/I balance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Calfa et al., 2011; Calfa et al., 2015.

claim: The Mecp2 KO mouse model exhibits hypoactivity of cortical regions.
source: We focused on the Mecp2 KO mouse model of RTT because of the heightened activity in the vHIP (Calfa et al., 2011; Calfa et al., 2015) and the hypoactivity of cortical regions (Durand et al., 2012; Kron et al., 2012; Morello et al., 2018; Sceniak et al., 2016; Tomassy et al., 2014), both resulting from opposite changes in their microcircuit E/I balance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Durand et al., 2012; Kron et al., 2012; Morello et al., 2018; Sceniak et al., 2016; Tomassy et al., 2014.

claim: All vHIP neurons in WT mice that interacted with live mice showed higher c-Fos intensities than those in mice that interacted with toy mice, irrespective of their efferent projections.
source: All vHIP neurons in WT mice that interacted with live mice showed higher c-Fos intensities than those in mice that interacted with toy mice, irrespective of their efferent projections [p<0.0001, Three-Way ANOVA followed by Benjamini and Hochberg Multiple Comparisons (B and H-MC); Figure 1D–E].
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data showing increased neuronal activity in vHIP neurons following social interactions, as shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons in WT mice that interacted with live mice had higher c-Fos intensities than those projecting to the LH.
source: Furthermore, mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons in WT mice that interacted with live mice had higher c-Fos intensities than those projecting to the LH (n = 275 mPFC-projecting neurons in six sections from four mice, n = 282/3/2 LH-projecting neurons; p=0.0022, Three-Way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data comparing mPFC-projecting and LH-projecting vHIP neurons.

claim: mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons in Mecp2 KO mice that interacted with live mice had higher c-Fos intensities than those interacting with toy mice.
source: We obtained similar results in Mecp2 KO mice, with higher c-Fos intensities in mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons of mice interacting with live mice compared to those interacting with toy mice (p=0.0034, Three-Way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC; Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data in Mecp2 KO mice, as shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The difference between mPFC- and LH-projecting vHIP neurons from mice that interacted with live mice was not statistically significant in Mecp2 KO mice, suggesting the loss of selectivity in vHIP signaling.
source: However, the difference between mPFC- and LH-projecting vHIP neurons from mice that interacted with live mice was not statistically significant, suggesting the loss of selectivity in vHIP signaling in Mecp2 KO mice (p=0.1544, Three-Way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC; Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data and statistical analysis, with interpretation provided by the authors.

claim: The PL region of the mPFC of Mecp2 KO mice had fewer c-Fos-positive neurons than that of WT mice that interacted with live mice.
source: Consistent with the lower levels of neuronal activity reported previously in the mPFC (Kron et al., 2012), the PL region of the mPFC of Mecp2 KO mice had fewer c-Fos-positive neurons than that of WT mice that interacted with live mice (p=0.0234, Two-Way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data in the mPFC and a citation to Kron et al., 2012.

claim: Both WT and Mecp2 KO mice that interacted with live mice had more c-Fos-positive neurons compared to those that interacted with toy mice.
source: However, both WT and Mecp2 KO mice that interacted with live mice had more c-Fos-positive neurons compared to those that interacted with toy mice, indicating that the mPFC of both genotypes is more robustly activated during a social encounter than by exposure to novel inanimate objects (p<0.05, Two-Way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data in the mPFC, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both WT and Mecp2 KO mice spent more time investigating the cup containing stranger one compared to the empty cup.
source: Both WT and Mecp2 KO mice spent more time investigating the cup containing stranger one compared to the empty cup. The discrimination index (DI) of this preference is statistically different than chance in both genotypes, and comparable between the two genotypes (n = 12 WT mice; n = 11 Mecp2 KO mice; One-sample t-test against chance p<0.0001 for both genotypes; Two-sample t-test p=0.3523; Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the three-chamber social test, as shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Social preference is intact in Mecp2 KO mice.
source: These data indicate that social preference is intact in Mecp2 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing that Mecp2 KO mice discriminate between a social target and an empty cup.

claim: WT mice spent more time investigating the cup containing stranger 2 in the social memory test.
source: Indicative of social memory for stranger one and their preference for novel mice, WT mice spent more time investigating the cup containing stranger 2 (n = 12 WT mice, p=0.0002, One-sample t-test; Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the three-chamber social memory test, as shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: The DI of Mecp2 KO mice in the social memory test was significantly different than that of WT mice, and not statistically different than chance.
source: However, the DI of Mecp2 KO mice was significantly different than that of WT mice, and not statistically different than chance (n = 11 Mecp2 KO mice; Two-sample t-test p=0.0140; One-sample t-test p=0.9436; Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating a deficit in the social memory of the stranger one mouse that was encountered 2 min before.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the three-chamber social memory test, as shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Mecp2 KO mice have a deficit in social memory.
source: However, the DI of Mecp2 KO mice was significantly different than that of WT mice, and not statistically different than chance (n = 11 Mecp2 KO mice; Two-sample t-test p=0.0140; One-sample t-test p=0.9436; Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating a deficit in the social memory of the stranger one mouse that was encountered 2 min before.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing that Mecp2 KO mice do not discriminate between familiar and novel mice in the social memory test.

claim: WT mice mainly engaged in following behavior in the unrestricted social interaction assay.
source: Unbiased scoring of social interactions by the machine-learning based Janelia Automatic Animal Behavior Annotator (JAABA) (Kabra et al., 2013; Ohayon et al., 2013; Robie et al., 2017) revealed that WT mice mainly engaged in following behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by automated behavioral scoring data from the unrestricted social interaction assay.

claim: Mecp2 KO mice followed and sniffed other mice significantly less than WT mice.
source: By contrast, Mecp2 KO mice followed and sniffed other mice significantly less than WT mice, but engaged in an atypical 'jumping on' behavior (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by automated behavioral scoring data from the unrestricted social interaction assay, as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mecp2 KO mice engaged in an atypical 'jumping on' behavior.
source: By contrast, Mecp2 KO mice followed and sniffed other mice significantly less than WT mice, but engaged in an atypical 'jumping on' behavior (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by automated behavioral scoring data from the unrestricted social interaction assay, as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mecp2 KO mice displayed less digging and facial grooming, more wall jumping, and more shuffled walking compared to WT mice.
source: In addition, Mecp2 KO mice displayed less digging and facial grooming, more wall jumping, and more shuffled walking (n = 11 WT mice, n = 11 Mecp2 KO mice, p<0.05, Student's t-test or Mann-Whitney test dependent on normalcy; Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by automated behavioral scoring data from the unrestricted social interaction assay, as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: WT and Mecp2 KO mice spent a comparable amount of time walking.
source: As a critical control for social interactions in the unrestricted arena and the three-chamber test, WT and Mecp2 KO mice spent a comparable amount of time walking (p=0.4135, Student's t-test; Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by automated behavioral scoring data from the unrestricted social interaction assay, as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: During the first 4 min of the unrestricted assay, WT mice preferentially interacted with the novel mouse across all measured social behaviors.
source: During the first 4 min of the unrestricted assay, WT mice preferentially interacted with the novel mouse across all measured social behaviors, including following, sniffing, and 'jumping on' (n = 11 mice, p<0.05, One-sample t-test; Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), after which social interaction declined regardless of the target mouse (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by automated behavioral scoring data from the unrestricted social interaction assay, as shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Mecp2 KO mice showed no significant preference between the familiar and novel mouse in the unrestricted social interaction assay.
source: The discrimination indices between WT mice and Mecp2 KO mice were significantly different (p<0.05, Two-sample t-test; Figure 2G), and indeed Mecp2 KO mice showed no significant preference between the familiar and novel mouse (n = 11 mice, p>0.05, One-sample; Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), consistent with previously observed deficits in social memory (see Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by automated behavioral scoring data from the unrestricted social interaction assay, as shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The amplitudes of VSD signals evoked by single pulse stimulation of vHIP afferents were larger in mPFC slices from Mecp2 KO mice compared to WT littermates at a range of stimulation intensities.
source: The amplitudes of VSD signals evoked by single pulse stimulation of vHIP afferents were larger in mPFC slices from Mecp2 KO mice compared to WT littermates at a range of stimulation intensities [n = 11 slices from 7 WT mice, n = 11/5 Mecp2 KO mice, p=0.0470, Two-way repeated measures (RM) ANOVA; Figure 3D and E].
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-sensitive dye imaging data showing enhanced vHIP-evoked responses in mPFC slices from Mecp2 KO mice, as shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: The spatiotemporal spread of VSD signals throughout the mPFC slice was similar between Mecp2 KO and WT mice.
source: The spatiotemporal spread of VSD signals throughout the mPFC slice was similar between Mecp2 KO and WT mice (p=0.4529, Two-way RM ANOVA; Figure 3F), although the spatial spread was significantly larger at lower stimulation intensities in slices from Mecp2 KO mice (p=0.0133, Mann-Whitney test; Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-sensitive dye imaging data, as shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Stimulating intracortical fibers evoked VSD amplitudes of comparable amplitude in slices from Mecp2 KO and WT mice.
source: Stimulating intracortical fibers with another theta glass electrode placed in layer 2/3 of the same cortical column evoked VSD amplitudes of comparable amplitude in slices from Mecp2 KO and WT mice (n = 11 slices from 7 WT mice, n = 11/5 Mecp2 KO mice, p=0.0540; Two-way RM ANOVA; Figure 3H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-sensitive dye imaging data, as shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: The spatiotemporal spread of VSD signals evoked by intracortical stimulation was significantly smaller in slices from Mecp2 KO mice.
source: By contrast, the spatiotemporal spread of VSD signals evoked by intracortical stimulation was significantly smaller in slices from Mecp2 KO mice (p=0.0498, Two-way RM ANOVA; Figure 3J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-sensitive dye imaging data, as shown in Figure 3J-K.

claim: vHIP inputs are overrepresented in the mPFC network of Mecp2 KO mice.
source: These data indicate that vHIP fibers drive hyperactivation of the mPFC network in Mecp2 KO mice, in contrast to the hypoactivation driven by intracortical stimulation, suggesting that vHIP inputs are overrepresented in the mPFC network of Mecp2 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the voltage-sensitive dye imaging data showing larger vHIP-evoked responses and smaller intracortical-evoked responses in Mecp2 KO mice.

claim: High-frequency stimulation of vHIP afferents evoked a significant potentiation of the spatiotemporal spread of VSD signals in mPFC slices from WT mice.
source: In mPFC slices from WT mice, high-frequency stimulation of vHIP afferents evoked a significant potentiation of the spatiotemporal spread of VSD signals, which persisted up to 45 min (n = 10 slices from seven mice, p=0.0013, Student's paired t-test, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and was sensitive to the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) antagonist APV (100 µM) (n = 4 slices from four mice, p=0.9205; Student's paired t-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-sensitive dye imaging data showing LTP at vHIP-mPFC synapses in WT mice, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: mPFC slices from Mecp2 KO mice showed only a short-term enhancement of the spatiotemporal spread of VSD signals after high-frequency stimulation.
source: However, mPFC slices from Mecp2 KO mice showed only a short-term enhancement of the spatiotemporal spread of VSD signals, which quickly decayed back to baseline levels (n = 9 slices from five mice, p=0.2705; Student's paired t-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-sensitive dye imaging data showing impaired LTP at vHIP-mPFC synapses in Mecp2 KO mice, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: LTP at excitatory vHIP-mPFC synapses is impaired in Mecp2 KO mice.
source: These data demonstrate an impairment of LTP at excitatory vHIP-mPFC synapses, similar to that previously reported at CA3-CA1 synapses in hippocampal slices of Mecp2 KO mice (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the voltage-sensitive dye imaging data and supported by a citation to Li et al., 2016.

claim: WT mice expressing the excitatory DREADD hM3Dq in mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons and treated with CNO had a significantly lower DI in the unrestricted social assay, which was not different than chance.
source: CNO-treated WT mice expressing the excitatory DREADD hM3Dq in mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons (to mimic vHIP hyperactivity in Mecp2 KO mice) had a significantly lower DI, which was not different than chance (n = 12, One-way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC, p=0.0287; One-sample t-test, p=0.6905; Figure 4C), indicating a deficit in social memory resembling that of Mecp2 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by chemogenetic manipulation and behavioral data, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Chronic inhibition of mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons with the inhibitory DREADD hM4Di caused a significant decrease in the DI and impaired social memory in WT mice.
source: Chronic inhibition of mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons with the inhibitory DREADD hM4Di also caused a significant decrease in the DI and impaired social memory in WT mice (n = 9, One-way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC, p=0.0081; One-sample t-test, p=0.3332;) (Figure 4C), underscoring the role of this long-range projection in social memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by chemogenetic manipulation and behavioral data, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Inhibiting mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons in Mecp2 KO mice with the inhibitory DREADD hM4Di was sufficient to increase the time following the novel mouse compared to the familiar littermate in 73% of the treated Mecp2 KO mice.
source: This manipulation was sufficient to increase the time following the novel mouse compared to the familiar littermate in 73% of the treated Mecp2 KO mice, resulting in a significant preference for the novel mouse, and indicating a rescue of social memory (n = 15, One-sample t-test, p=0.0312, Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by chemogenetic manipulation and behavioral data, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The amount of time performing the atypical 'jumping on' behavior did not differ between hM4Di-expressing and mCherry control Mecp2 KO mice.
source: For example, the amount of time performing the atypical 'jumping on' behavior did not differ between hM4Di-expressing and mCherry control Mecp2 KO mice (p>0.9999 within genotypes; p<0.05 between genotypes; Kruskal-Wallis test followed by Dunn's Multiple Comparisons; Figure 4D), suggesting that the vHIP-mPFC projection plays a specific role in the memory aspect of social interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The vHIP-mPFC projection plays a specific role in the memory aspect of social interactions.
source: For example, the amount of time performing the atypical 'jumping on' behavior did not differ between hM4Di-expressing and mCherry control Mecp2 KO mice (p>0.9999 within genotypes; p<0.05 between genotypes; Kruskal-Wallis test followed by Dunn's Multiple Comparisons; Figure 4D), suggesting that the vHIP-mPFC projection plays a specific role in the memory aspect of social interactions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing that chemogenetic manipulation affects social memory but not other social behaviors.

claim: WT mice expressing the excitatory DREADD hM3Dq in mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons had larger vHIP-induced VSD signals in mPFC slices compared to mCherry-expressing WT controls.
source: Consistent with their deficit in social memory, WT mice expressing the excitatory DREADD hM3Dq in mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons had larger vHIP-induced VSD signals in mPFC slices compared to mCherry-expressing WT controls, resembling those observed in mCherry-expressing Mecp2 KO controls (n = 18 slices from 9 mCherry WT mice; n = 12/8 hM3Dq WT; n = 17/8 Mecp2 KO mice; p<0.0001; p=0.6530; Two-way RM ANOVA; Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-sensitive dye imaging data, as shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Inhibiting mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons with hM4Di did not affect vHIP-induced VSD signals in mPFC slices of WT mice.
source: Surprisingly, inhibiting mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons with hM4Di did not affect vHIP-induced VSD signals in mPFC slices of WT mice (p=0.0642; Figure 4E-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-sensitive dye imaging data, as shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Social memory DI was negatively correlated with the amplitude of vHIP-induced VSD signals in mPFC slices from hM4Di-expressing Mecp2 KO mice on a mouse-per-mouse basis.
source: This analysis uncovered a statistically significant negative correlation between DI and vHIP-induced mPFC responses (n = 7 pairs, r = −0.7895 p=0.0347, Spearman r correlation; Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between behavioral and electrophysiological data, as shown in Figure 4I.

claim: vHIP-induced VSD signals in mPFC slices from Mecp2 KO mice that showed improved social memory after expression of hM4Di in mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons were smaller than those in mCherry-expressing Mecp2 KO controls.
source: Furthermore, vHIP-induced VSD signals in mPFC slices from Mecp2 KO mice that showed improved social memory after expression of hM4Di in mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons were smaller than those in mCherry-expressing Mecp2 KO controls (n = 11/6, p<0.0001, Two-way ANOVA; Figure 4J–K), resembling those in mCherry-expressing WT mice (p=0.3043).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-sensitive dye imaging data, as shown in Figure 4J-K.

claim: vHIP-induced VSD signals in mPFC slices from Mecp2 KO mice that still showed deficits in social memory after expression of hM4Di in mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons were significantly larger than those in mCherry-expressing WT mice.
source: By contrast, vHIP-induced VSD signals in mPFC slices from Mecp2 KO mice that still showed deficits in social memory after expression of hM4Di in mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons were significantly larger than those in mCherry-expressing WT mice (p<0.0001; Two-way ANOVA; Figure 4J–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-sensitive dye imaging data, as shown in Figure 4J-K.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the social memory DI and the amplitude of VSD signals evoked by intracortical stimulation in hM4Di-expressing Mecp2 KO mice.
source: Importantly, there was no significant correlation between the social memory DI and the amplitude of VSD signals evoked by intracortical stimulation in hM4Di-expressing Mecp2 KO mice (n = 7 pairs, r = −0.1519, p=0.7451, Spearman r correlation; Figure 4I), and no difference in these signals between Mecp2 KO mice that showed improvement in social memory and those that did not (n = 11/6 Memory; n = 6/4 No memory; p=0.3359; Two-way RM ANOVA; Figure 4L–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis and voltage-sensitive dye imaging data, as shown in Figure 4I and 4L-M.

claim: Acute excitation of mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons by CNO activation of hM3Dq impaired social memory in WT mice.
source: These i.p. CNO injections did not affect social memory in mCherry-expressing WT mice as their DI was significantly higher than chance (n = 10, p=0.009, One-sample t-test), whereas acute excitation of mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons by CNO activation of hM3Dq impaired social memory in WT mice (n = 10 hM3Dq WT mice, p=0.7775, One-sample t-test; Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by acute chemogenetic manipulation and behavioral data, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Acute inhibition of mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons with the inhibitory DREADD hM4Di in Mecp2 KO mice caused them to have a significant preference for the familiar mouse.
source: Intriguingly, acute inhibition of mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons with the inhibitory DREADD hM4Di in Mecp2 KO mice caused them to have a significant preference for the familiar mouse (n = 6, p=0.0004, One-sample t-test Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and show a difference in DI compared to mCherry expressing Mecp2 KO mice whose DI was not different than chance (n = 10, p=0.8081, One-sample t-test; mCherry vs. hM4Di Mecp2 KO p=0.0197, One-Way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC).
evidence: This claim is supported by acute chemogenetic manipulation and behavioral data, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: WT mice expressing the excitatory DREADD hM3Dq in mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons showed the same discrimination for the novel object as control mCherry-expressing mice in the novel object recognition test.
source: WT mice expressing the excitatory DREADD hM3Dq in mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons showed the same discrimination for the novel object as control mCherry-expressing mice 2 hr after a single i.p. injection of CNO (n = 8 WT mCherry mice, p=0.0058; n = 10 hM3Dq, p=0.0172; One-sample t-test; mCherry vs. hM3Dq p=0.3524; Two-sample t-test; Figure 5C–D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating that altering the activity of the long-range vHIP-mPFC projection does not affect hippocampal-dependent novel object recognition.
evidence: This claim is supported by chemogenetic manipulation and behavioral data, as shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Altering the activity of the long-range vHIP-mPFC projection does not affect hippocampal-dependent novel object recognition.
source: WT mice expressing the excitatory DREADD hM3Dq in mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons showed the same discrimination for the novel object as control mCherry-expressing mice 2 hr after a single i.p. injection of CNO (n = 8 WT mCherry mice, p=0.0058; n = 10 hM3Dq, p=0.0172; One-sample t-test; mCherry vs. hM3Dq p=0.3524; Two-sample t-test; Figure 5C–D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating that altering the activity of the long-range vHIP-mPFC projection does not affect hippocampal-dependent novel object recognition.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing no effect of vHIP-mPFC manipulation on novel object recognition.

claim: Both hM3Dq-expressing and mCherry-expressing WT mice had a significant preference for the novel mouse compared to the familiar mouse when NAc-projecting vHIP neurons were manipulated.
source: Both hM3Dq-expressing and mCherry-expressing WT mice had a significant preference for the novel mouse compared to the familiar mouse and were not different from each other (n = 10 WT mCherry mice, p=0.00058; n = 11 WT hM3Dq mice, p=0.072; One-sample t-test; mCherry vs. hM3Dq p=0.6294; Two-sample t-test; Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), indicating that mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons, but not NAc-projecting vHIP neurons, are necessary for the expression of social memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by chemogenetic manipulation and behavioral data, as shown in Figure 5F.

claim: mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons, but not NAc-projecting vHIP neurons, are necessary for the expression of social memory.
source: Both hM3Dq-expressing and mCherry-expressing WT mice had a significant preference for the novel mouse compared to the familiar mouse and were not different from each other (n = 10 WT mCherry mice, p=0.00058; n = 11 WT hM3Dq mice, p=0.072; One-sample t-test; mCherry vs. hM3Dq p=0.6294; Two-sample t-test; Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), indicating that mPFC-projecting vHIP neurons, but not NAc-projecting vHIP neurons, are necessary for the expression of social memory.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing that manipulation of vHIP-NAc projections does not affect social memory.

claim: In WT mice, the majority of WGA-labeled, NeuN-positive cells were projection pyramidal neurons, with 52% being IT neurons and 37% PT neurons.
source: In WT mice, the majority of WGA-labeled, NeuN-positive cells were projection pyramidal neurons, with 52% being IT neurons and 37% PT neurons, followed by 4% PV interneurons, 2% CAL interneurons, and 1% SOM interneurons (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by trans-synaptic tracing and immunohistochemistry data, as shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The fraction of PT pyramidal neurons was significantly smaller in Mecp2 KO mice (16%).
source: The fraction of PT pyramidal neurons was significantly smaller in Mecp2 KO mice (16%) (n = 9 sections from three mice for both WT and Mecp2 KO mice, p=0.0128, Student's t-test), whereas the fraction of PV interneurons was significantly larger in Mecp2 KO mice (9%) (p=0.0477, Student's t-test; Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by trans-synaptic tracing and immunohistochemistry data, as shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The fraction of PV interneurons was significantly larger in Mecp2 KO mice (9%).
source: The fraction of PT pyramidal neurons was significantly smaller in Mecp2 KO mice (16%) (n = 9 sections from three mice for both WT and Mecp2 KO mice, p=0.0128, Student's t-test), whereas the fraction of PV interneurons was significantly larger in Mecp2 KO mice (9%) (p=0.0477, Student's t-test; Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by trans-synaptic tracing and immunohistochemistry data, as shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In the mPFC of WT mice, PT pyramidal neurons were preferentially innervated by vHIP axons.
source: In the mPFC of WT mice, PT pyramidal neurons were preferentially innervated by vHIP axons (index = 2.1104, n = 9 sections from three mice, p=0.0001, one-sample Student's t-test; Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by trans-synaptic tracing and immunohistochemistry data, as shown in Figure 6G.

claim: vHIP axons innervated PV cells in the mPFC of Mepc2 KO mice more than in WT mice.
source: By contrast, vHIP axons innervated PV cells in the mPFC of Mepc2 KO mice more than in WT mice (n = 9/3, p=0.0425, Student's t-test), to the detriment of PT pyramidal cells (n = 9/3, p=0.0161, Student's t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by trans-synaptic tracing and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: The pattern of innervation of vHIP axons in the mPFC changes from mainly targeting excitatory projection pyramidal neurons in WT mice to preferentially targeting PV-expressing inhibitory GABAergic interneurons in Mecp2 KO mice.
source: Combined, these results indicate that the pattern of innervation of vHIP axons in the mPFC changes from mainly targeting excitatory projection pyramidal neurons in WT mice to preferentially targeting PV-expressing inhibitory GABAergic interneurons (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the trans-synaptic tracing and immunohistochemistry data, as shown in Figure 6G-H.

claim: The numerical densities of mCherry-expressing en passant presynaptic terminals belonging to vHIP neurons and those belonging to c-mPFC neurons were comparable between WT and Mecp2 KO mice across all cortical layers of the mPFC.
source: The numerical densities of mCherry-expressing en passant presynaptic terminals belonging to vHIP neurons and those belonging to c-mPFC neurons were comparable between WT and Mecp2 KO mice across all cortical layers of the mPFC (p>0.05, Two-way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC; Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis of presynaptic boutons, as shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The weighted size of individual presynaptic boutons of vHIP axons in layer 5 of the mPFC was significantly larger in Mecp2 KO mice.
source: However, the weighted size of individual presynaptic boutons of vHIP axons in layer 5 of the mPFC was significantly larger in Mecp2 KO mice (n = 993 boutons in WT mice, n = 664 Mecp2 KO mice, p<0.0001, Two-way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC), though there was no difference in layer 2/3 (n = 543 boutons in WT mice, n = 720 in Mecp2 KO mice, p=2565, Two-way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC; Figure 7G–H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis of presynaptic boutons, as shown in Figure 7G-H.

claim: The sizes of presynaptic boutons of c-mPFC axons in layer 5 were significantly smaller in Mecp2 KO mice.
source: In contrast, the sizes of presynaptic boutons of c-mPFC axons in layers five were significantly smaller in Mecp2 KO mice (n = 782 WT mice, n = 575 Mecp2 KO mice, p=0.0133; Two-way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC, Figure 7G–H), though not in layer 2/3 (n = 698 WT, n = 818 Mecp2 KO, p=8422, Two-way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis of presynaptic boutons, as shown in Figure 7G-H.

claim: Presynaptic boutons of vHIP axons in layer 5 of the mPFC were significantly smaller than those of c-mPFC axons in WT mice.
source: Interestingly, presynaptic boutons of vHIP axons in layer 5 of the mPFC were significantly smaller than those of c-mPFC axons in WT mice, a difference absent in Mecp2 KO mice due to larger vHIP boutons and smaller c-mPFC boutons (WT, p<0.0001; Mecp2 KO 0.2320; Figure 7G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis of presynaptic boutons, as shown in Figure 7G-H.

claim: The amplitude of red light vHIP-evoked EPSCs was significantly larger in pyramidal neurons from Mecp2 KO mice compared to those from WT mice at all ranges of light pulse durations.
source: The amplitude of red light vHIP-evoked EPSCs was significantly larger in pyramidal neurons from Mecp2 KO mice compared to those from WT mice at all ranges of light pulse durations (n = 17 cells in 6 slices from 6 WT mice; n = 11/5/5 Mecp2 KO mice; p=0.0118; Two-way RM ANOVA; Figure 8C), whereas the amplitude of vHIP-evoked monosynaptic EPSCs in layer five interneurons (identified by their size, shape, input resistance, and capacitance; see Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–D) was comparable in both genotypes (n = 11 cells in 7 slices from 7 WT mice; n = 12/9/9 Mecp2 KO mice; p=0.4327; Two-way RM ANOVA; Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation and whole-cell recording data, as shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The amplitude of vHIP-evoked monosynaptic EPSCs in layer five interneurons was comparable in both WT and Mecp2 KO genotypes.
source: The amplitude of red light vHIP-evoked EPSCs was significantly larger in pyramidal neurons from Mecp2 KO mice compared to those from WT mice at all ranges of light pulse durations (n = 17 cells in 6 slices from 6 WT mice; n = 11/5/5 Mecp2 KO mice; p=0.0118; Two-way RM ANOVA; Figure 8C), whereas the amplitude of vHIP-evoked monosynaptic EPSCs in layer five interneurons (identified by their size, shape, input resistance, and capacitance; see Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–D) was comparable in both genotypes (n = 11 cells in 7 slices from 7 WT mice; n = 12/9/9 Mecp2 KO mice; p=0.4327; Two-way RM ANOVA; Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation and whole-cell recording data, as shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Blue light stimulation of Chronos-expressing c-mPFC axons evoked EPSCs of comparable amplitude in both layer five pyramidal neurons and interneurons from WT and Mecp2 KO mice at all ranges of light pulse durations.
source: In contrast, blue light stimulation of Chronos-expressing c-mPFC axons evoked EPSCs of comparable amplitude in both layer five pyramidal neurons and interneurons from WT and Mecp2 KO mice at all ranges of light pulse durations (p=0.1617; p=0.6129; Two-way RM ANOVA; Figure 8E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation and whole-cell recording data, as shown in Figure 8E-F.

claim: vHIP-evoked EPSCs were larger in layer five pyramidal neurons from Mecp2 KO mice compared to WT mice when normalized to c-mPFC-evoked EPSCs (103% vs. 54%).
source: The cell-by-cell normalization of the amplitude of EPSCs evoked by red light stimulation of Chrimson-expressing vHIP axons to the amplitude of EPSCs evoked by blue light stimulation of Chronos-expressing c-mPFC axons revealed that vHIP-evoked EPSCs were larger in layer five pyramidal from Mecp2 KO mice compared to WT mice (103% vs. 54%; p=0.00083; Two-way RM ANOVA; Figure 8G).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation and whole-cell recording data, as shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Normalized EPSC amplitudes in interneurons were not significantly different between Mecp2 KO and WT mice (97% vs. 81%).
source: In contrast, normalized EPSC amplitudes in interneurons were not significantly different between Mecp2 KO and WT mice (97% vs. 81%; p=0.3208; Two-way RM ANOVA) (Figure 8H).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation and whole-cell recording data, as shown in Figure 8H.

claim: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio of EPSCs evoked by red light vHIP stimulation was larger in layer five pyramidal neurons from Mecp2 KO mice compared to those from WT mice.
source: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio of EPSCs evoked by red light vHIP stimulation was larger in layer five pyramidal neurons from Mecp2 KO mice compared to those from WT mice (n = 11 cells from six slices from WT mice; n = 13/5/5 Mecp2 KO mice; p=0.0114; Two-way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC), whereas the AMPAR/NMDAR ratio of EPSCs evoked by blue light c-mPFC stimulation was smaller in Mecp2 KO mice compared to WT mice (p=0.0114; Two-way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC; Figure 8J).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation and whole-cell recording data, as shown in Figure 8J.

claim: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio of EPSCs evoked by blue light c-mPFC stimulation was smaller in Mecp2 KO mice compared to WT mice.
source: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio of EPSCs evoked by red light vHIP stimulation was larger in layer five pyramidal neurons from Mecp2 KO mice compared to those from WT mice (n = 11 cells from six slices from WT mice; n = 13/5/5 Mecp2 KO mice; p=0.0114; Two-way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC), whereas the AMPAR/NMDAR ratio of EPSCs evoked by blue light c-mPFC stimulation was smaller in Mecp2 KO mice compared to WT mice (p=0.0114; Two-way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC; Figure 8J).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation and whole-cell recording data, as shown in Figure 8J.

claim: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio of EPSCs evoked by either vHIP or c-mPFC stimulation in interneurons was not significantly different between Mecp2 KO and WT mice.
source: In contrast, the AMPAR/NMDAR ratio of EPSCs evoked by either vHIP or c-mPFC stimulation in interneurons was not significantly different between Mecp2 KO and WT mice (n = 9/7/7 WT mice; n = 11/9/9 Mecp2 KO mice; p=0.8843 vHIP stimulation; p=0.8121 c-mPFC stimulation; Two-way ANOVA followed by B and H-MC; Figure 8K).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation and whole-cell recording data, as shown in Figure 8K.

claim: vHIP excitatory synapses are selectively stronger on layer five pyramidal neurons, but not interneurons, in the mPFC of Mecp2 KO mice.
source: Combined, these results demonstrate that vHIP excitatory synapses are selectively stronger on layer five pyramidal neurons, but not interneurons, in the mPFC of Mecp2 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the optogenetic stimulation and whole-cell recording data showing larger EPSCs and higher AMPAR/NMDAR ratios at vHIP-mPFC synapses onto pyramidal neurons but not interneurons.
